item.title: Trump administration sanctions International Criminal Court
item.description:
Trump administration sanctions International Criminal Court

October 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The United States has announced sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), escalating Trump’s war on the international tribunal.

“We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate,” US secretary of state Marco Rubio said in an announcement.

The Trump administration has previously pledged to dismantle the court “brick by brick” and has sanctioned 13 current and former staff members, but this is the first time it has levied sanctions against the institution itself.

Ahead of the announcement, prime minister Rob Jetten said the Netherlands will protect the ICC “stone by stone”.

Foreign minister Tom Berendsen said the country would stand behind the court. “The announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court are an undesirable new escalation,” Berendsen said in a statement. “I deeply regret this new step.”

The sanctions will cut the court off from any US company or organisation, including providers of financial and technology services.

The announcement came hours after South African jurist Navi Pillay, who has served as a judge at both the ICC and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

Trump has long coveted the prize, telling reporters earlier this week that he deserved the award for what he said was ending eight wars.

item.title: Russia wants NL to hand over ICC judges
item.description:
Russia wants NL to hand over ICC judges

October 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Russia has asked the Netherlands to hand over nine International Criminal Court (ICC) officials who were convicted in absentia last year.

The prosecutor’s office in Moscow requested the extradition of the court’s president, Tomoko Akane, and other staff members for their involvement in the arrest warrant of Russian president Vladimir Putin.

The ICC issued the warrant for Putin’s alleged involvement in “the war crime of unlawful deportation of children” from occupied Ukraine.

The ICC has also issued an arrest warrant against Maria Alekseyevna Lvova-Belova, Russia’s commissioner for children’s rights.

In December, a court in Moscow convicted Akane and others in absentia, sentencing them to prison terms ranging from 3.5 to 15 years.

Japan, Akane’s home country, said the request was regrettable. “Measures targeting individuals connected to the ICC are unjust and unacceptable,” Masanao Ozaki, the country’s deputy chief cabinet secretary, said.

The United States has also sanctioned 13 staff members, including Akane, over the investigation into alleged Israeli war crimes in Gaza.

item.title: Unions call regional transport strike, threaten weekly walkout
item.description:
Unions call regional transport strike, threaten weekly walkout

October 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Regional bus services across the Netherlands will be heavily disrupted on Wednesday, after the FNV and CNV unions called a nationwide 24-hour strike in a dispute over a new pay and conditions deal.

If Wednesday’s strike does not shift the employers, the unions say they will hold an action day every week, and will only announce the dates shortly beforehand. Earlier this month they said they were considering weekly strikes in the run-up to Christmas.

Some 13,000 workers, mainly bus drivers, are covered by the public transport collective agreement, which expired on July 1. Staff at Arriva, EBS, Qbuzz, Keolis, Transdev and RET’s regional services are involved. City transport in Amsterdam, Rotterdam and The Hague is not affected.

Talks broke down after eight rounds of negotiations. This week an ultimatum to the employers’ organisation VWOV expired without a response.

“Employers are holding on to drastic cuts in working conditions,” FNV negotiator Marijn van der Gaag said in a statement. “In doing so, they are forcing their staff to take action.”

The unions say employers want to reduce sick pay, add more unpaid breaks to shifts and give staff less say over their rosters. Rosters are currently fixed about eight days in advance, and employers want to cut that to four days or less, Van der Gaag said.

The FNV wants a 6% pay rise. The CNV is calling for 9.5% over two years, as well as better arrangements for older workers and faster access to permanent contracts.

“We will not let employers sabotage the action by drawing up emergency rosters at the last minute,” CNV negotiator Niels Rook said, explaining why dates will not be announced in advance.

item.title: Former ICC judge Navi Pillay awarded Nobel Peace Prize
item.description:
Former ICC judge Navi Pillay awarded Nobel Peace Prize

October 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

South African jurist Navi Pillay, who has served as a judge at both the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her efforts to promote peace and international law.

Most recently, the 85-year-old chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel had committed genocide.

Announcing the prize in Oslo, Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said it was going to someone who “held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict”.

Reacting to the news in Nuremberg, Pillay said “if you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”

The award comes as the system of international justice is under attack. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has threatened to dismantle the International Criminal Court “brick by brick, if necessary”, and the US has sanctioned several of its staff.

Pillay played a significant role in the anti-apartheid movement in her homeland as a defence lawyer for Nelson Mandela and other activists. She went on to serve as a judge on the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, spending the last four of her eight years there as its president.

She was one of the ICC’s first judges, sitting in the appeals chamber from 2003 until 2008, when she stepped down to become UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.

In 2019, she was appointed as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice by the Gambia, which had filed genocide proceedings against Myanmar over its treatment of the Rohingya minority.

Last year, as chair of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, she said Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

In a post on social media, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen congratulated Pillay. “Few have devoted their lives to justice, peace and human dignity like she did,” she said.

The prize is administered by the Nobel Foundation and comes with 12 million Swedish kronor (around €1.07 million).

item.title: Museums, festivals and clubs in Groningen ban smart glasses
item.description:
Museums, festivals and clubs in Groningen ban smart glasses

October 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

In a joint statement on Friday some 30 cultural organisations in Groningen announced they were banning the use of smart glasses from their buildings and events.

The devices, the most popular version is sold by Meta, look like normal glasses but allow users to film and take photos covertly.

“This technology compromises the privacy and safety of visitors, staff, and artists, and undermines trust in an open, respectful environment,” the statement says.

Backers including the Groninger Archieven, the Groninger Museum, Noorderlicht, Stichting Kunst & Cultuur and the Grand Theatre Groningen.

Last week, eyewear chain Hans Anders announced it would stop selling Meta camera glasses following demands from privacy advocates concerned about the so-called “pervert glasses”.

Dutch privacy watchdog AP has warned that sharing images made with camera glasses violates GDPR laws unless permission is given by everyone in the images.

The consumer watchdog Consumentenbond has also issued a warning about the glasses, noting that it was possible to manipulate or cover the indicator light to make it even harder to tell images were being captured.

MPs have called for a full ban on the glasses but the cabinet is opposed to a blanket measure and wants to see other restrictions put into place.

Utrecht music venue Tivoli Vredenburg banned smart glasses at its events in 2025 and has since refused entry to one man who would not take them off.

item.title: NL’s only legal medicinal cannabis grower goes bust
item.description:
NL’s only legal medicinal cannabis grower goes bust

October 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Patients who use medicinal cannabis face having to switch to imported products after the only licensed grower in the Netherlands was declared bankrupt on Thursday.

A court in Groningen declared Veendam-based Bedrocan bankrupt two weeks after the company had applied for protection from its creditors. The firm, whose main growing site is in Emmeloord, employs around 70 people.

Bedrocan ran into trouble after the health ministry ended its contract at the start of this year. All medicinal cannabis sold in Dutch pharmacies is bought and distributed by the state-run Bureau for Medicinal Cannabis (BMC).

The ministry ended the deal in anticipation of a change in the law that will let growers sell directly to pharmacies. But health minister Sophie Hermans (VVD) told MPs in July that the change is not expected to take effect until July 1, 2028.

That left Bedrocan unable to supply the BMC and not allowed to sell to pharmacies itself, the Volkskrant reported. The state was by far its largest customer.

Limited stockpile
The BMC built up a stockpile of Bedrocan cannabis before the contract ended, but the minister said it was limited and had a finite shelf life. The BMC will switch to imported cannabis during 2027, with products matching current THC and CBD levels as closely as possible.

Around 7,000 people in the Netherlands are prescribed medicinal cannabis, according to the Volkskrant. They include people with multiple sclerosis (MS), severe pain, certain forms of epilepsy, and patients in palliative care.

Patients fear a different variety will not work as well for them. Cannabis contains many compounds that together determine its effect, and the mix depends on the plant and how it is grown.

The MS association has written to Hermans warning that some long-term patients depend on a specific variety.

Bedrocan also supplied patients in other European countries through the BMC. The BMC is due to stop exporting at the end of 2026. In September, Bedrocan told foreign pharmacies and wholesalers to order from it directly.

item.title: MPs vote to fly rainbow flag at parliament for first time
item.description:
MPs vote to fly rainbow flag at parliament for first time

October 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The rainbow flag will fly at the Dutch parliament building on Sunday, Coming Out Day, after MPs overturned a decision by managers of parliament to drop the plan.
MPs backed the move by 90 votes to 36 in a vote late on Thursday night, public broadcaster NOS reported.

Parliament’s presidium, which runs its day-to-day affairs, initially agreed to the plan but changed its mind after Christian parties were told about the plan, RTL Nieuws reported on Thursday.

The orthodox Protestant SGP led the objections. “The rainbow flag is not a national flag but a flag of interest groups, which has grown into a symbol of activism,” SGP MP Diederik van Dijk told NOS.

Roll-call vote
Kati Piri, MP for opposition party Pro, then tabled a motion saying parliament should “stand up for the rights of the global LGBTI movement” and ensure “an inclusive working environment” for its staff.

Van Dijk responded by demanding a roll-call vote, in which each MP votes individually rather than by party. That meant MPs who had already gone home on Thursday had to return to The Hague.

Most MPs from D66, the VVD, CDA, PRO, PvdD, SP, ChristenUnie, 50PLUS and Volt voted in favour. The anti-immigration PVV, far-right Forum for Democracy (FVD), Denk and the SGP voted against, while MPs from JA21 and the Markuszower group were absent.

Purple Friday
The vote came on the eve of Purple Friday (Paarse Vrijdag), when schools mark LGBTI acceptance. This year it is being held in October for the first time, having been moved from December at the request of schools.

A record 3,130 schools have signed up, including 2,130 primary schools, compared with 2,890 last year, LGBTI rights organisation COC told news agency ANP.

The COC linked the rise to a survey published last month that found acceptance of homosexuality has slumped among teenagers. Only 22% of secondary school boys and 51% of girls now have a positive view, down from 40% and 78% in 2021.

item.title: MPs push for legal changes after pro-Hamas demonstration on Dam
item.description:
MPs push for legal changes after pro-Hamas demonstration on Dam

October 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

MPs are calling for a bill criminalising support for terrorist organisations to be pushed through faster, after demonstrators carried a “We support Hamas” banner onto the Dam on October 7, the third anniversary of the attacks in Israel.

Police and prosecutors judged that doing so was not illegal under current law. Police later stopped the marchers from heading towards the city’s Jewish quarter, home to the Portuguese Synagogue, the Jewish Museum and the Holocaust Names Monument.

Around 150 people were part of the group, according to Het Parool, with some chanting “Long live the 7th of October”. Some also carried a banner from the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PLFP), which is also on the EU terrorist list.

Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema described the event “shocking and distasteful” but noted that the protests were not illegal.

Protestors only have to notify a local council to hold a demonstration, and authorities can stop or intervene in one if it poses a threat to local safety or order.

Rival political figures have criticised the lack of intervention on Halsema’s part, with JA21 MP Ingrid Coenradie branding the decision to allow the protest “appalling”.

Orthodox Protestant SGP MP Diederik van Dijk submitted written questions to the justice minister David Van Weel asking why the protest was not broken up sooner.

A bill is already in parliament, submitted by Van Weel in June, proposing 3 new offences: glorifying the most serious terrorist crimes, distributing material that glorifies them, and publicly expressing support for banned terrorist organisations, which would carry a maximum sentence of 2 years in prison.

Van Weel amended the bill to meet objections from coalition party D66, which had long opposed it, so that support would only be punishable if it is aimed at winning others over to an organisation’s terrorist goals.

Peace organisation PAX has called for the bill to be scrapped, warning the law could be used against activists, journalists and protesters, and pointed to developments in the UK.

There, at least 3,070 people had been arrested by the end of April this year for showing support for Palestine Action, after the government banned the group as a terrorist organisation.

In 2024, around 320 people were arrested in Amsterdam after Halsema broke up a pro-Palestinian protest held on the same day as an October 7 commemoration on the Dam.

item.title: Maastricht area plans 30 care zones to tackle loneliness
item.description:
Maastricht area plans 30 care zones to tackle loneliness

October 9, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A new plan by care agencies and insurance companies aims to create 30 residential care zones in the Maastricht-Heuvelland area of Limburg, combining health services, activities and accessible living.

The plan, known as the Deltaplan Maastricht Heuvelland, aims to help older people live independently for longer and receive support and care closer to home, largely to tackle loneliness.

The initiative is a collaboration between municipalities, health insurers, residents, hospitals and elderly care advocacy agencies. Health insurers CZ and VGZ have provided €33.4 million for the project.

Nineteen of the 30 zones are currently under development, and organisers say the rest will be up and running next year.

“We have traditionally been accustomed to looking to nursing homes, but in this way, older people can continue living at home much longer, provided it is responsible,” Petra Lamberts, chair of Deltaplan, told regional news outlet L1.

The zones will also organise more activities, for example in a shared communal living room, to tackle loneliness. “Loneliness is a predictor of the need for care,” Lamberts told broadcaster NOS. “People notice minor ailments sooner when they are alone. When they take part in activities, they are distracted, and they are also encouraged to use their skills.”

Informal carers, such as family members, will also be able to hand over some of their tasks from time to time so they do not become overburdened.

A communal living room recently opened in Valkenburg, where local residents can take part in activities and meet for coffee.

The population of the region is ageing faster than the rest of the country. By 2030, one in four residents of South Limburg will be over 65.

According to Lamberts, a year of home care costs around €12,000, while a year in a nursing home costs more than €100,000.
